stories.title: Five-developer JV scores $96M construction loan for Coconut Creek apartments
stories.excerpt: A joint venture between five developers nabbed a $96 million construction loan for an apartment project in Coconut Creek. CIBC Bank USA provided the financing to 13th Floor Investments, Rockpoint, Rosemurgy Properties, Giles Capital Group and Schmier Property Group, the South Florida Business Journal reported.  The joint venture is developing Lutea at Mainstreet, a five-story residential project that’s part of a 200-acre master-planned community on the west side of Lyons Road between Wiles Road and West Samples Road. Plans call for 404 units, a pool with cabanas, a two-story fitness center, a rooftop speakeasy, a lounge, a kid’s room, a […]This article originally appeared on The Real Deal. Click here to read the full story.
bullets: JV of 5 developers scores $96M construction loan from CIBC for Coconut Creek 404-unit project
Lutea at Mainstreet first residential phase of $1B master-planned community; 2,360 total units planned
Breakground Jan 2027; completion late 2028; site includes retail, healthcare anchor (UM Health)
stories.summary: A five-developer JV (13th Floor Investments, Rockpoint, Rosemurgy, Giles Capital, Schmier) secured $96M in construction financing from CIBC Bank USA for Lutea at Mainstreet, a 404-unit apartment community in Coconut Creek. The project is the first residential phase of a $1B mixed-use development on 200 acres that will ultimately include 2,360 units, 100K SF retail, and a 300K SF healthcare campus anchored by University of Miami Health System. Groundbreaking is set for January 2027, with delivery in late 2028.
stories.impact: South Florida multifamily development remains well-capitalized despite higher rates; major healthcare anchor (UM Health) signals institutional confidence in Coconut Creek submarket. First-mover residential phase in large master-plan typically commands pricing power and sets tone for absorption; monitor healthcare campus timing, as employment draw (clinical/admin roles) will drive secondary wave of rental demand in Broward County.

stories.title: This Holiday Season, New York City Retail’s Split Recovery Reaches a Critical Point
stories.excerpt: The last mile is the hardest, and New York City’s retail sector is flagging near the finish line. Peter Braus, president and principal owner of Lee & Associates NYC, sees a retail market balancing two extremes. On one hand, it’s becoming increasingly hard to find the right space in the right area. One of Braus’s current clients, a “very strong” Italian brand seeking a New York City home in SoHo or along Madison Avenue, is in an especially competitive spot. The client’s preferred storefront in SoHo, for which it already had a lease out, just received a second offer. “The landlord is encouraging us to put in another offer,” Braus said. “It’s just incredibly competitive to find good space, and we’re seeing rents at levels that we haven’t seen for a really long time.” Just a few subway stops away, however, is the other end of the market spectrum, where vacancies stretch along corridors, like Broadway between City Hall and Tribeca, which Braus called “a disaster.” “I live in that area,” Braus said. “On a couple of blocks, all the stores are vacant from north to south.” New York City has nearly 142,000 storefronts, and an estimated 16,047 were vacant as of September, according to the Office of the New York City Comptroller’s recently launched vacancy dashboard. Retail vacancy citywide rose in the third quarter to 11.32 percent –– unwelcome news on the eve of the retail world’s most crucial shopping season. The citywide retail vacancy figure has hovered stubbornly between 11 percent and 11.6 percent since the third quarter of 2023, and remains above the last pre-pandemic measure of 10.5 percent. Five neighborhoods continue to see vacancies at a rate of around one in five stores, including Manhattan’s Financial District and Tribeca, Brooklyn’s Ocean Hill, and East New York and Queens’ Old Astoria-Hallets Point. Manhattan, in particular, faces some of the city’s most enduring retail vacancies, currently measuring at 13.12 percent. “What we’re seei
bullets: NYC retail split recovery: prime SoHo/Madison storefronts highly competitive; rents at multi-year highs
Secondary corridors (Broadway City Hall–Tribeca) face vacancy crisis; simultaneous scarcity and oversupply
Implications for mixed-use development rents and ground-floor economics remain uncertain
stories.summary: New York City's retail market is bifurcating sharply. Premium locations like SoHo and Madison Avenue command record rents and fierce competition (e.g., luxury Italian brand competing for single storefront), while nearby secondary corridors such as Broadway between City Hall and Tribeca are plagued by persistent vacancies. This two-speed recovery reflects flight to quality but masks underlying softness in lower-tier retail fundamentals.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact on multifamily: ground-floor retail in new residential projects will command premium rents only in highest-barrier submarkets (Soho, Upper East Side), making value-add harder in secondary NYC neighborhoods. Developers should assume lower retail lease rates and longer lease-up periods outside Manhattan core; this pressure may flow into unit rents if retail underperformance erodes project economics.

stories.title: Miami OKs Rosso and Vadia’s $2B Midtown Park project
stories.excerpt: Carlos Rosso and Alex Vadia secured city approval for their $2 billion Midtown Park mixed-use project, laying the groundwork for condos, retail, offices and amenities in the neighborhood. City commissioners approved a major use special permit that clears the way for the developers to raise 924 residential units, 120,000 square feet of retail, 60,000 square feet of office and a padel club at 3055 North Miami Avenue, the South Florida Business Journal reported. The project would include 2 acres of parks and total about 1.2 million square feet. Rosso Development and Midtown Development are partners on the project, which will […]This article originally appeared on The Real Deal. Click here to read the full story.
bullets: Carlos Rosso/Alex Vadia secure city approval for $2B Midtown Park mixed-use project in Miami
924 residential units across 4 towers (28, 28, 17, 17 stories); first phase 280-unit condo tower by mid-2029
Condo pricing starts low $600K; 2 acres parks; Gramercy Park–inspired model signals residential-led development
stories.summary: Rosso Development and Midtown Development secured city approval for Midtown Park, a $2B mixed-use project at 3055 North Miami Avenue delivering 924 residential units, 120K SF retail, 60K SF office, and 2 acres of parks across four phases. The first phase is a 280-unit condo tower designed by Arquitectonica, with units from studios to penthouses starting in the low $600Ks and delivery by 2029. The project replaces a failed Walmart site and was inspired by New York's Gramercy Park model.
stories.impact: Major Miami Midtown residential catalyst: 924-unit pipeline signals developer confidence in neighborhood despite rental market softness elsewhere in Miami. Condo-led (not rental) first phase reduces near-term rental supply pressure but may cannibalize rental demand in Midtown submarket; monitor whether Phase 2–4 pivot to rental or remain for-sale. Mixed-use density and park amenities will attract talent and service workers, supporting secondary rental demand in adjacent neighborhoods.

stories.title: In Long Island Real Estate in 2027, Tight Supply Will Be a Key Driver
stories.excerpt: As 2027 approaches, real estate development on Long Island presents a mix of challenges and opportunities. Interest rates moved higher in 2026, and tighter lending standards have placed additional pressure on project financing. We expect financing costs to stay at or above current levels through 2027. Yet, Long island’s underlying market fundamentals remain strong, particularly in sectors where demand continues to outpace supply. Limited housing inventory and opportunities to reposition well-located aging commercial properties will continue to support investment across the region. Capital has not disappeared. Long Island investment sales reached $1.8 billion in the first half of 2026, up 21.2 percent year-over-year, according to Cushman & Wakefield. But lenders and investors will remain selective, favoring disciplined underwriting and experienced developers who understand the local market. Project selection will be critical as developers balance long-term demand against current financing costs. Scott Burman. Photo: Courtesy Burman. Housing is where we expect the most activity in 2027. Multifamily demand remains strong, supported by limited inventory, affordability challenges, and Long Island’s rapidly growing population of adults age 65 and older, underscoring the need for a broader range of housing options. Policy is beginning to help as well. 2027 will also mark the first full year under New York’s 2026 SEQRA reforms, which are designed to streamline environmental review for qualifying housing developments without overriding local zoning and permitting requirements. Another major opportunity is repositioning. According to Schuckman Realty, Long Island retail vacancy was 4.2 percent in mid-2026, asking rents were up about 9 percent year-over-year, and virtually no new retail space was being built. In a market this tight, the opportunity lies in transforming aging and underutilized commercial properties, particularly traditional shopping malls, into destinations
bullets: Long Island 2027 outlook: tight housing inventory, strong multifamily fundamentals despite higher rates
2026 SEQRA reforms streamline permitting for housing; first full year of benefits in 2027
Limited supply + aging population 65+ + affordability crisis = tailwind for new rental and senior housing
stories.summary: Long Island's real estate market in 2027 will benefit from tight housing inventory and strong underlying demand despite higher interest rates and tighter lending standards. The state's 2026 SEQRA (State Environmental Quality Review Act) reforms, which streamline environmental review for qualifying housing projects, take full effect in 2027. Multifamily demand remains robust, driven by limited inventory, affordability challenges, and rapid growth in the 65+ population, creating opportunities for new construction and repositioning of aging commercial assets.
stories.impact: SEQRA streamlining is a major tailwind for Long Island multifamily starts in 2027; developers should front-load land acquisition and preliminary design now to capture first-mover advantage before permitting backlogs reappear. Aging population signals strong senior housing (55+ rentals, assisted living conversions) opportunity; repositioning old retail/office into workforce housing aligns with policy priorities. Expect financing to remain tight; bulk up equity and secure pre-approvals early.

stories.title: Mamdani Scores Critical Court Victory for Rent Freeze
stories.excerpt: Just ahead of the Thanksgiving weekend, a Manhattan Supreme Court judge sided with New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani on his controversial rent freeze in a case that landlords brought against the New York City Rent Guidelines Board (RGB). The mayor called the decision “a victory for tenants, for affordability and for the principle that working New Yorkers deserve a city they can afford to live in.” The case stems from a 7-1 vote by the mayor-appointed RGB on June 26 halting rent increases for the city’s approximately 1 million rent-stabilized apartments. The judge in today’s ruling, Brendan T. Lantry, emphasized that his decision was not a vote for or against the wisdom of the RGB’s ruling, and that it “may cause negative collateral consequences,” but that the rent freeze was nevertheless legal. In a lawsuit filed in July, landlords had contended that the RGB ignored evidence of the rising expenses that rent-stabilized owners face in maintaining and upgrading their buildings. In some cases, the landlords said, the RGB ignored its own data, which “clearly signaled a rent increase,” according to Ann Korchak, board president of Small Property Owners of New York, whose members were plaintiffs in the lawsuit. “This ruling is terribly disappointing to small property owners,” Korchak said in a statement on Wednesday. “The rent freeze will push more small rent-stabilized property owners to the edge of the cliff. It denies the resources they need to maintain and operate their rent-stabilized buildings. Property taxes, water and sewer rates, and insurance, energy, heating, repair and other costs and expenses aren’t frozen. Rents should not be frozen, either.” Randy Mastro, a lawyer for the landlords in the case, said in a statement to Commercial Observer that they were “disappointed by the court’s ruling.” “The judge acknowledged multiple irregularities in the RGB’s process and, in particular, called out Mayor Mamdani’s ‘comments, promises and guarant
bullets: NYC court upholds Mayor Mamdani's rent freeze for 1M rent-stabilized units; RGB 7-1 vote validated
Judge acknowledged freeze may cause 'negative collateral consequences' but ruled it legal
Rent-stabilized segment locked; impact on new construction and market-rate rents TBD
stories.summary: Manhattan Supreme Court Judge Brendan T. Lantry upheld Mayor Zohran Mamdani's controversial rent freeze imposed by the NYC Rent Guidelines Board in June, which halted rent increases for approximately 1 million rent-stabilized apartments citywide. The judge acknowledged the decision may have adverse effects but found it legally sound. The ruling rejects landlord arguments that the RGB ignored rising operating expenses.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact on multifamily development: rent-stabilized stock is off-market and does not drive new construction underwriting. However, frozen rents on 1M units reduce landlord cash flow and may depress resale values, limiting capital recycling for upgrades or reinvestment. Market-rate rents (90%+ of new construction) remain unaffected, but regulatory overhang may dampen investor appetite for NYC multifamily and push capital to Sunbelt markets with clearer rent-setting frameworks.

stories.title: Netflix Acquiring Historic Radford Studio Center for $380M
stories.excerpt: Netflix has reached an agreement to acquire the historic Radford Studio Center in Studio City for a reported $380 million, marking the streaming giant’s first purchase of a Los Angeles-area studio lot. The property is located at 4024 Radford Avenue, just off Ventura Blvd in the southeastern San Fernando Valley, close to Hollywood, Burbank and many other entertainment-related businesses. As reported by the L.A. Times and other sources, Goldman Sachs took control of the property in January after its previous owner, Hackman Capital Partners, defaulted on a $1.1 billion mortgage amid a slowdown in Hollywood production. Hackman and Square Mile Capital Management acquired the property for $1.85 billion in 2021. The 1.14 million-square-foot production campus features 22 soundstages, 18 office buildings and 20 bungalows. Founded in 1928 by filmmaker Mack Sennett, the studio has been home to numerous iconic television series, including Seinfeld, Gilligan’s Island, Will & Grace and The Mary Tyler Moore Show. The acquisition represents a significant expansion of Netflix’s Southern California real estate holdings. The company currently leases approximately 2 million square feet of office and soundstage space in Los Angeles. Netflix intends to retain Radford’s existing studio team and maintain operations at the production campus. bullets: Netflix acquires Radford Studio Center (1.14M SF, 22 soundstages) for $380M in Los Angeles
Goldman Sachs seized property after Hackman Capital defaulted on $1.1B mortgage in 2026
Netflix now controls ~2M SF of LA production space; expands beyond leasing to ownership
stories.summary: Netflix has agreed to purchase the historic Radford Studio Center in Studio City, Los Angeles, for $380 million. The 1.14 million-square-foot production campus (22 soundstages, 18 offices, 20 bungalows) was foreclosed by Goldman Sachs in January 2026 after the previous owner, Hackman Capital Partners, defaulted on a $1.1B mortgage amid Hollywood production slowdown. The acquisition marks Netflix's first studio lot purchase and expands its Southern California real estate footprint to approximately 2M SF.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily impact; however, Netflix's $380M investment signals confidence in LA entertainment industry recovery and may stabilize San Fernando Valley real estate values. Hackman's default was a harbinger of distress in LA media real estate; Netflix's acquisition removes a large distressed asset from market and reduces fire-sale risk. San Fernando Valley studio district may see ancillary demand for workforce housing (crew, below-the-line talent) if production ramps; monitor for multifamily plays near Radford, Burbank, and Glendale.

stories.title: Fairstead Closes $17M Affordable Housing Transaction in Oklahoma
stories.excerpt: Fairstead announced its $16.5 million acquisition of London Square Village Apartments, a 200-unit project-based Section 8 community in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, and plans for a comprehensive rehabilitation of the property. The transaction marks Fairstead’s first acquisition in Oklahoma. London Square Village Apartments consists of 200 units across 18 two-story residential buildings and a community center. The community includes 24 one-bedroom, 96 two-bedroom and 80 three-bedroom homes, with all units reserved for households earning at or below 60% of the area median income.  “Expanding into Oklahoma represents an important step in Fairstead’s mission to preserve sustainable, reliable affordable housing for communities across the country,” said Jeff Goldberg, Founder and CEO of Fairstead. The acquisition will preserve London Square Village Apartments as affordable housing through 4% federal LIHTC equity from R4 Capital and tax-exempt bond financing issued by the Oklahoma Housing Finance Agency, with R4 Capital also serving as lender. Join us for the Connect Midwest Multifamily conference on the afternoon of Tuesday, June 8, 2027, at Joe’s Live in Rosemont, Illinois. The post Fairstead Closes $17M Affordable Housing Transaction in Oklahoma appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Fairstead acquires London Square Village Apartments (200-unit Section 8) in Oklahoma City for $16.5M
All units reserved for households earning ≤60% AMI; 4% LIHTC + tax-exempt bonds finance
Fairstead's first Oklahoma acquisition; preservation and rehabilitation play
stories.summary: Fairstead closed its first acquisition in Oklahoma, purchasing London Square Village Apartments—a 200-unit project-based Section 8 community in Oklahoma City earning at or below 60% area median income—for $16.5M. Financing includes 4% federal LIHTC equity from R4 Capital and tax-exempt bond financing from the Oklahoma Housing Finance Agency. The acquisition includes plans for comprehensive property rehabilitation.
stories.impact: Minimal impact on market-rate multifamily development. This is a preservation/LIHTC play targeting subsidized stock; it signals long-term investor confidence in Oklahoma City and validates tax credit market. However, it does not indicate market-rate rental demand strength. Developers should note: Oklahoma tax credit market is maturing and attracting national operators, suggesting stable (if modest) financing availability; acquisition prices suggest cap rates ~5–6%, consistent with low-yielding affordable housing.

stories.title: Dwight Capital Finances $52M Loan for Mixed-Use Multifamily Community in Michigan
stories.excerpt: Dwight Capital has closed a $52 million HUD 223(f) loan for Griffin Royal Oak, a 245-unit luxury mixed-use multifamily community in the heart of Royal Oak, Michigan. Developed by Singh Development, the property features a five-story residential building, an attached parking garage, and four ground-floor commercial spaces totaling 9,000 square feet. Strategically located near downtown Royal Oak, Griffin Royal Oak is surrounded by pedestrian-friendly sidewalks, boutiques, salons, and retail shops, and more than 70 restaurants. The property’s luxury residences, ground-floor retail, and walkable location reflect Singh Development’s focus on thoughtfully designed communities in desirable locations. “Griffin Royal Oak represents the type of community we have focused on developing for more than five decades—high-quality residential environments in strong, established markets,” said Saab Grewal of Singh Development. Dwight Capital’s Karnveer Bal and Alex Shoenfeld originated the loan on behalf of Singh Development, an established, family-owned real estate development and investment company. Join us for the Connect Midwest Multifamily conference on the afternoon of Tuesday, June 8, 2027, at Joe’s Live in Rosemont, Illinois. The post Dwight Capital Finances $52M Loan for Mixed-Use Multifamily Community in Michigan appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Dwight Capital closes $52M HUD 223(f) loan for Griffin Royal Oak, 245-unit mixed-use in Michigan
Singh Development project; 5-story tower + 9K SF ground retail in downtown Royal Oak
Walkable urban location, strong amenity/dining ecosystem supports luxury positioning
stories.summary: Dwight Capital has closed a $52 million HUD 223(f) refinance/acquisition loan for Griffin Royal Oak, a 245-unit luxury mixed-use multifamily community developed by Singh Development in Royal Oak, Michigan. The property features a five-story residential building, parking garage, and 9,000 SF of ground-floor retail, positioned in downtown Royal Oak's pedestrian-friendly, restaurant-rich district. Singh Development, a family-owned operator active for 50+ years, is known for high-quality residential environments in strong markets.
stories.impact: HUD 223(f) availability confirms stable debt market for stabilized multifamily outside major metros. Royal Oak (Detroit metro) represents secondary-market demand resilience; strong walkability and retail ecosystem support rent stability. Developers eyeing Midwest secondary metros should model HUD loan availability as primary debt source; it offers lower rates but longer holds. Singh's focus on 'thoughtfully designed communities' in 'strong, established markets' signals developer focus on operational efficiency over growth; expect modest rent growth in Royal Oak but low turnover risk.

stories.title: TSMC eyes 3K-acre Aggieland site for $22.6B chip plant
stories.excerpt: Taiwan-based TSMC is sizing up a slice of land in Aggieland to build a $23 billion chipmaking plant.  TSMC tipped their hand through a Texas Jobs, Energy, Technology and Innovation program application that revealed some details for the proposed campus.  TSMC estimates that the proposed semiconductor manufacturing plant in College Station will generate $64 billion over a four decade operating period, according to the Houston Business Journal, who cited the application. If the project gets the green light, construction would be set to begin in 2027 and conclude some time in 2031. The project is expected to employ nearly 10,000 […]This article originally appeared on The Real Deal. Click here to read the full story.
bullets: TSMC eyes 3,000-acre site in College Station, Texas for $22.6B semiconductor plant; Texas comptroller approved
10,000 construction jobs (2027–31); 2,000 permanent operations jobs; $64B economic impact over 40 years
Negotiation phase; TSMC also considering Arizona; real estate broker agreement in place
stories.summary: Taiwan-based TSMC has received formal approval from the Texas comptroller for a potential $22.6 billion semiconductor manufacturing plant on 3,000 acres in College Station (Brazos County). The facility would generate 10,000 construction jobs over five years (2027–2031), 2,000 permanent jobs, and an estimated $64 billion in economic impact over 40 years. The state could realize $326 million in tax revenue during construction and $3B+ over the facility's 40-year operating life. TSMC maintains optionality, also considering an Arizona site.
stories.impact: Transformational demand catalyst for College Station and Central Texas multifamily. TSMC plant would create immediate construction-period demand (2027–31) for workforce housing near the site, then sustained demand from 2,000+ permanent employees + families and their supply chain. Early movers should secure land near College Station NOW for workforce/market-rate builds timed for 2027–2028 starts. Monitor for infrastructure announcements (roads, utilities, schools); major capex projects typically precede large employer buildout. If TSMC commits, expect 3–5 year runway for multifamily absorption and rent growth in Brazos County; model similar to Austin's tech boom but with more compressed timeline.

stories.title: Host Hotels Rounds Out $202M Brooklyn Hotel Buy With $29M Retail, Parking Acquisition
stories.excerpt: Host Hotels & Resorts has secured three retail spaces and an indoor parking area at its newly acquired hotel asset in Brooklyn’s Dumbo neighborhood. The Bethesda, Md.-based real estate investment trust, through the entity Brooklyn Bridge Hotel Owner, acquired the commercial condo units and parking space at 90 Furman Street from a Starwood Capital Group entity, according to property records filed Wednesday. All four properties were built in 2015, according to city tax records, and adjoin Host Hotel’s newest portfolio addition, 1 Hotel Brooklyn Bridge at 60 Furman Street. Host Hotel acquired the hotel’s 85-year leasehold interest from Starwood in a $202 million all-cash deal announced earlier this month. The 195-key hotel marks a significant feather in Host Hotel’s cap, as the operator expects 1 Hotel Brooklyn Bridge to be among its top 10 assets based on full-year estimates. A second agreement, this one concerning the takeover and restructuring of an existing $113 million debt on the properties at 90 Furman and 60 Furman Street, was also filed in city records Wednesday. The properties’ existing mortgage was previously held by Sumitomo Mitsui Banking, according to the filing, and has now been assigned to the entity TRS NY Lender. The same entity has previously been linked by The Real Deal to the New York State Teachers’ Retirement System of NYC, which financed Host Hotels’ 2024 purchase of Starwood’s 1 Hotel Central Park at 1414 Avenue of the Americas. That $265 million deal was in one of that year’s top 10 investment sales. Host Hotels’ recent acquisition of the Dumbo hotel came on the heels of a $127 million all-cash purchase of the 308-room Renaissance Dallas at Plano Legacy West Hotel in Texas. The seller was a joint venture of Paceline Equity Partners and Aravest. Spokespeople for Host Hotels and Starwood did not respond to requests for comment. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Host Hotels acquires 85-year leasehold at 1 Hotel Brooklyn Bridge (195 keys) for $202M all-cash
Adds 3 retail + parking condo units at 90 Furman Street for $29M; restructures $113M debt
Hotel positioned as top-10 Host asset; Dumbo waterfront submarket desirable for hospitality
stories.summary: Host Hotels & Resorts acquired the 85-year leasehold interest in 1 Hotel Brooklyn Bridge (195 keys, 60 Furman Street) in Dumbo for $202 million all-cash, then separately acquired adjacent retail and parking condos at 90 Furman Street for $29M from a Starwood Capital Group entity. Host also restructured $113M in existing debt on both properties. Host expects the hotel to rank among its top 10 assets based on full-year performance projections.
stories.impact: Limited multifamily impact. Hotel acquisition in Dumbo is a hospitality play; however, it signals strong capital availability for high-barrier NYC waterfront assets and validates Dumbo's status as top-tier tourist/hospitality destination. This may indirectly pressure nearby multifamily rents (workers drawn to hospitality jobs) but also increases gentrification risk and raises construction costs through labor competition. Developers in Dumbo/DUMBO-adjacent should model higher wage inflation and longer lease-up timelines due to hospitality competition for workforce.

stories.title: Thor Equities Buys San Francisco Office/Retail Asset for $50.5M, Lands $51.8M Loan
stories.excerpt: Thor Equities has acquired 55 Stockton Street, a boutique Class A office and retail property in San Francisco’s Union Square district, from Zaber Corporation for $50.5 million. The company also secured $51.8 million in acquisition financing from Prime Finance. Also known as the National Center Building, the eight-story, 136,714-square-foot property is situated at the corner of Stockton and O’Farrell streets, one block south of Union Square. Built in 1988 and renovated in 2023, the building features three floors of retail space with boutique office space above. Office tenants include Chalk AI, Harness and Taylor & Associates Architects. The acquisition expands Thor’s presence in the Union Square district. The firm acquired nearby 146 Geary St., home to Bang & Olufsen’s flagship store, for $20.5 million in August. Thor also owns 152 Geary St., occupied by Banana Republic. The property offers convenient access to public transportation and is surrounded by prominent retail, dining and hospitality destinations. Newmark’s Chris Kramer, Ricky Braha, Tim Polglase and Dante DiStefano arranged the financing on behalf of Thor Equities. The post Thor Equities Buys San Francisco Office/Retail Asset for $50.5M, Lands $51.8M Loan appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Thor Equities buys 55 Stockton Street (136.7K SF, Class A office/retail, Union Square) for $50.5M
Secured $51.8M financing from Prime Finance; 8-story 1988-built, 2023 renovated
Expands Thor's Union Square portfolio (also owns 146 Geary, 152 Geary)
stories.summary: Thor Equities acquired 55 Stockton Street (the National Center Building), a 136,714 SF Class A office/retail property in San Francisco's Union Square, for $50.5M and secured $51.8M in acquisition financing from Prime Finance. Built in 1988 and renovated in 2023, the property features three floors of retail and boutique office space. The acquisition expands Thor's presence in Union Square, where it already owns 146 Geary and 152 Geary.
stories.impact: No direct multifamily impact. Thor's Union Square consolidation signals confidence in SF office-retail mixed-use but does not reflect strong office fundamentals (national office vacancy remains elevated). Retail is performing better than office; Thor is betting on street-level retail to anchor leasing. Multifamily developers in SF should note: office weakness limits worker population growth, moderating rental demand outside tech-heavy neighborhoods (SOMA, Mission Bay); Union Square area may see slower rent growth than Central/East SF.

stories.title: OC Investor Group Buys Two Apartment Properties in Venice
stories.excerpt: A group of private Orange County-based investors acquired two multifamily properties totaling 40 units in the coastal Los Angeles community of Venice for $14.23 million. The properties, located at 1400 and 1500 Venice Blvd., were sold by Advanced Real Estate Group. The transaction, which partly included 1031 exchange capital, worked out to $355,662 per unit and $430 per square foot. Colliers’ Kitty Wallace represented the seller and, along with colleague Andy Eberhard, also represented the buyers. Built in 1988 and 1985, respectively, the properties encompass 33,072 square feet of building area and offer 77 parking spaces. Neither property is subject to the City of Los Angeles Rent Stabilization Ordinance. The 31-unit property at 1400 Venice Blvd. features renovated interiors, a fitness center, a rooftop lounge and subterranean parking. The nine-unit property at 1500 Venice Blvd. sold above its asking price for approximately $3.43 million, representing a 5.13% capitalization rate. The new ownership plans to continue the previous ownership’s unit renovation program. Photo is of 1500 Venice Blvd. The post OC Investor Group Buys Two Apartment Properties in Venice appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Orange County investor group buys two Venice (LA) multifamily properties, 40 units total, for $14.23M
1400 Venice Blvd. (31 units, $355K/unit); 1500 Venice Blvd. (9 units, 5.13% cap); not RSO-covered
1988 and 1985 vintage; new ownership plans to continue unit renovation program
stories.summary: A group of private Orange County investors purchased two multifamily properties totaling 40 units in Venice, Los Angeles, for $14.23 million ($355,662 per unit). The 31-unit property at 1400 Venice Blvd. sold with renovation amenities (fitness center, rooftop lounge); the 9-unit property at 1500 Venice Blvd. sold at a 5.13% cap rate. Neither property is covered by the LA Rent Stabilization Ordinance. The 1988 and 1985 built properties (33K SF total) are slated for continued renovation under new ownership.
stories.impact: Small-dollar, operational-efficiency play in coastal LA submarket; indicates OC-based investor confidence in Venice rental fundamentals but not a strong growth signal. 5.13% cap rate on 9-unit property is reasonable for unencumbered LA coastal asset; suggests cap rates holding in $350–360K/unit range for vintage multifamily in Venice. Developers should note: Venice remains supply-constrained and non-RSO, allowing rent growth; however, micro-property transactions (9 units) indicate consolidation pressure and potential slow bleed of smaller holdings into larger platforms. Limited new development play here; focus on value-add and hold-and-operate strategies.

stories.title: Goose grabs $135M construction loan in Gowanus
stories.excerpt: Yitzchok Katz’s Goose Property Management is going into the holiday week with 135 million reasons to celebrate. Affinius Capital provided the developer with $135 million in construction financing for a project in Brooklyn’s Gowanus neighborhood, the Commercial Observer reported. Galaxy Capital’s Henry Bodek arranged the debt. In a statement, Affinius executive director Perry Katz said the development at 172 Third Avenue was “well positioned to meet rental demand in Gowanus.” Katz also called attention to the development’s proximity to public transit. Goose closed on a deal to buy the Gowanus development site from Jack Elo’s Elo Organization two years ago; […]This article originally appeared on The Real Deal. Click here to read the full story.
bullets: Yitzchok Katz's Goose Property Management secures $135M construction loan from Affinius for Gowanus 280-unit project
172 Third Avenue; three buildings, 8–14 stories, studios to 2-bed, 8.5K SF retail; major transit access
Goose also closing $143M loan for Park Slope Arrow Linen site (396 units, four 10-story buildings)
stories.summary: Goose Property Management secured $135 million in construction financing from Affinius Capital for a three-building, 280-unit apartment development at 172 Third Avenue in Gowanus. The project consists of 8–14 story buildings with studios to two-bedroom units, 8,500 SF of retail, and significant residential amenities. Goose acquired the vacant site from Elo Organization for $22M two years ago. Concurrently, Goose closed $143M financing from Affinius for a four-building, 396-unit development at the former Arrow Linen site in Park Slope.
stories.impact: Affinius is actively financing large Gowanus/Park Slope pipeline (combined $278M on 676 units), signaling strong lender confidence in Brooklyn's industrial-turn submarkets. Gowanus and Park Slope are supply-constrained with transit access; rent growth will likely track 3–5% annually as buildings deliver. Developers should recognize: (1) Gowanus is now 'proved' submarket (multiple major builds financed and underway), enabling faster lease-up; (2) Affinius's willingness to stack $135M + $143M suggests high carry capacity and institutional confidence; (3) retail components (8.5K SF + Arrow retail) must lease quickly or bleed cash. Monitor lease-up timeline; if retail stalls, may signal broader Brooklyn retail softness.

stories.title: Flight to Quality Deepens Divide Among Major U.S. Office Markets
stories.excerpt: The U.S. office market is showing more signs of improvement, but the recovery remains uneven across the nation’s biggest cities. The national office vacancy rate declined 140 basis points annually to 17.2 percent in October, while average asking rents increased 1.5 percent to $33.30 per square foot, according to a report using Yardi data. Office sales totaled nearly $56.9 billion across 2,576 transactions through the first 10 months of 2026, with properties trading at an average of $197 per square foot. But the flight to quality is widening the performance gap between newer and older properties, the report found. Asking rents for Class A office space increased 2.5 percent over the past year, while rents for Class B space declined 0.3 percent. “Office employment growth doesn’t always translate into an office market rebound, and we are seeing significant market discrepancies,” Peter Kolaczynski, director of Yardi Research, said in the report. “One consistency, though, is that outdated and less amenitized buildings are facing the most pressure, while new deliveries are offering best-in-class product and obtaining rent premiums.” Manhattan led the nation’s largest office markets in investment volume, construction activity, asking rents and occupancy in October. Investors traded more than $6.2 billion worth of Manhattan office properties in the first 10 months of the year at an average of $533 per square foot. Meanwhile, Manhattan’s average asking rents increased 9.5 percent annually to $74.44 per square foot, more than double the national average. The borough also had 3.73 million square feet of office space under construction, the largest development pipeline in the country. Miami recorded the strongest annual office rent growth among the markets tracked, with asking rates jumping 12.8 percent to $63.58 per square foot. The South Florida market’s office-using employment increased 22.1 percent since January 2021, while its office inventory expanded just 5.3 percen
bullets: US office vacancy declined 140 bps YoY to 17.2% (Oct 2026); asking rents +1.5% to $33.30/SF
Class A rents +2.5% YoY; Class B rents –0.3% YoY; 'flight to quality' widening performance gap
Office sales $56.9B (2,576 txns) through Oct 2026; average price $197/SF; outdated buildings face pressure
stories.summary: The U.S. office market is stabilizing selectively, with national vacancy declining 140 basis points year-over-year to 17.2% and asking rents rising 1.5% to $33.30/SF through October 2026. However, performance is highly uneven: Class A office rents increased 2.5% while Class B rents declined 0.3%, reflecting a sharp 'flight to quality.' Office sales totaled $56.9B on 2,576 transactions, with average pricing at $197/SF, but older, less amenitized buildings face the most pressure.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily impact, but signals broader CRE capital flows. Flight to quality in office suggests institutional capital is NOT deployed in older, less-liquid assets; this capital is competing for newer multifamily. Expect higher cap rate compression and fiercer bidding wars for new/recently renovated multifamily in high-barrier markets (Class A office submarkets typically overlap with strong multifamily). Dated office buildings may fuel adaptive-reuse (office-to-residential conversion), creating supply in select markets; monitor conversion pipelines in secondary metros (Class B office to multifamily).

bullets: Miami permits 39-story Brickell Starlite residential tower (517 units, $159M valuation); $250M construction loan closed

All three projects are actively financed and moving to or through construction.
stories.impact: South Florida multifamily pipeline remains robust and well-capitalized despite higher rates. Three major towers (517 + 448 + 208 = 1,173 units) represent continued confidence in Miami/Edgewater/Aventura submarkets. Affinius and Natixis are primary lenders, indicating institutional debt availability. However, pace of deliveries (2028–2029 likely) will compress rents if absorption is slow; monitor pre-leasing velocity on Brickell Starlite and Edgewater projects. Early-stage developers should secure financing commitments NOW; lender appetite is strong but competition for allocation is fierce.

bullets: Yoni Sade (Sade Real Estate) converts 40-story River Oaks apartment tower to 114-unit Raffles branded condos
2929 Weslayan Street; average unit 3,300 SF; targeting mid-2028 opening; units starting ~$3M
Modeled after St. Regis Residences Houston ($220M, 2029 delivery, units from $3.5M)
stories.summary: Developer Yoni Sade is converting the 40-story apartment tower at 2929 Weslayan Street in River Oaks into a 114-unit Raffles-branded luxury condo building. Units will average 3,300 SF with pricing starting just under $3 million, targeting mid-2028 delivery. Sade was inspired by the success of the nearby St. Regis Residences Houston ($220M, 40K+ SF amenities, units from $3.5M, 2029 delivery), where penthouse pricing reached $14.5M. Raffles marks the Singapore luxury hotel brand's Texas entry.
stories.impact: Apartment-to-branded-condo conversion signals speculative shift in luxury Houston market: developers betting on condo sales (higher per-unit revenue, one-time capital event) vs. rental NOI. River Oaks is premier submarket; conversion success depends on absorption and mortgage financing availability for $3M+ units. If conversions absorb quickly (2027–2028), expect follow-on conversions in other Houston luxury towers; if stalled, signals oversupply and risk of condo-to-rental fallback. Rental developers should monitor: each condo conversion removes rental supply, tightening Houston market and supporting rent growth, but also signals capital flight to for-sale (less equity/debt for rental).
